title: Global pauser cannot freeze BalancerPoolerV2.pool(); emergency response gap
description: BalancerPoolerV2.pool() is gated by Pausable.whenNotPaused, whose pause state is controlled by ATokenDispatcherV2.pause()/unpause(), which is in turn gated by onlyMinter (NFTMinterV2). NFTMinterV2 only flips that pause via setDispatcherActive(), which is onlyOwner. The Global Pauser exposed through NFTMinterV2.pause()/unpause() (lines L111-L122) is a separate paused flag inside NFTMinterV2 that ONLY gates _executeMint via 'require(!paused)' on L171. It does NOT propagate to the dispatcher's own Pausable. Therefore, when the Global Pauser pauses NFTMinterV2 in an incident, BalancerPoolerV2.pool() remains callable by any authorized pooler. An authorized pooler (operational bot) can still execute swaps, sendTo, redeems, and add-liquidity against the real Balancer V3 vault while the rest of the system is frozen. The owner has to take a separate transaction (setDispatcherActive(dispatcher,false)) to actually freeze pool(). In a fast-moving incident (e.g., compromised pooler key, anomalous pool state, sUSDS / waUSDC oracle desync) the gap between Global Pause and dispatcher pause is exactly the window where pool() is most dangerous to leave open.
exploit_path:
1. Global Pauser detects an incident (e.g., compromised pooler key, observed swap manipulation on the live sUSDS/waUSDC pool) and calls NFTMinterV2.pause(). The mint surface is now frozen.
2. BalancerPoolerV2 is NOT paused — its internal Pausable._paused is still false. pool() remains callable.
3. The compromised pooler (or an attacker who already triggered the pause condition) calls pool(minBPT=0, minUSDC=0). The unlockCallback executes against the live Balancer V3 vault: real swap, real sendTo, real redeem, real addLiquidity — with zero slippage guarding because the attacker controls the args.
4. Owner is the only party that can stop this; until owner sends setDispatcherActive(dispatcher,false), the attacker can drain accumulated sUSDS into the donation path or sandwich themselves on the LP add.

The gap is not theoretical — it is the entire point of having two pause layers. The system pretends Global Pause covers everything but it actually only covers minting.
mainnet_realism_check: Does not rely on any mock behaviour. The Balancer V3 Vault at 0xbA1333333333a1BA1108E8412f11850A5C319bA9 will happily execute the unlock/swap/settle/addLiquidity sequence regardless of NFTMinterV2's internal pause flag — the vault has no knowledge of the dispatcher's external pause status. Likewise real waUSDC.redeem and sUSDS.deposit are unaffected by an upstream NFTMinterV2 pause. The pause-coverage gap is a property of the contract code, not of the AMM.
recommendation: Either (a) have NFTMinterV2.pause() iterate registered dispatchers and call dispatcherContract.pause() on each (and unpause on resume), or (b) add a second whenNotPaused check on pool() that consults NFTMinterV2(minter).paused(), or (c) introduce a shared PauseRegistry that BalancerPoolerV2.pool() consults. Whichever approach is chosen, document the pause topology so operators know which switch freezes which surface.
severity_rationale: Downgraded from initial Medium guess to Low/QA. The dispatcher CAN be halted — just via a different control plane (`NFTMinterV2.setDispatcherActive(dispatcher, false)`, owner-only) rather than the global Pauser role. The Global Pauser halts NFTMinterV2._executeMint; the dispatcher pause is a separate, owner-controlled flag. So pool() is not unstoppable — it just has a slower, owner-mediated halt path rather than the faster Pauser-role halt that operators may assume covers everything. This is a pause-topology / operator-mental-model issue: an operator may incorrectly believe Global Pause freezes pool(), when in fact they must additionally request the owner call setDispatcherActive. The exploit path requires a window of operator-misunderstanding plus a compromised pooler or adverse market window — multiple compounding assumptions. Per C4 QA/Low: 'State handling, function incorrect as to spec, issues with comments. Governance/Centralization risk including admin privileges.' This is a documentation/topology gap that should be addressed in the runbook and code comments, not a direct security failure.
